questions.question: Explain the difference between population distribution and population density.
questions.expected_answer: Population distribution is the way people are spread out over an area, the pattern of where they live, which can be shown on a dot map or shaded map, with densely and sparsely populated areas. Population density is the average number of people living in each square kilometre, a measure of how crowded a place is, worked out by dividing the population by the area.

questions.question: Calculate the population density of a town with twenty thousand people and an area of ten square kilometres, and explain what South Africa's average density tells us.
questions.expected_answer: Population density equals population divided by area, so twenty thousand divided by ten equals two thousand people per square kilometre. South Africa had about sixty-two million people on about one point two million square kilometres, so its average density is about fifty people per square kilometre. But this is only an average: parts of Gauteng and townships have thousands per square kilometre, while parts of the Northern Cape have fewer than one.

questions.question: Describe and explain the population distribution of South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: People are clustered in Gauteng, around Durban and the KwaZulu-Natal coast, around Cape Town, Gqeberha and East London, and in parts of Limpopo, Mpumalanga and the Eastern Cape, while the Northern Cape, Karoo and western Free State are sparsely populated. The east is wetter and better for farming, Gauteng and port cities have many jobs, and under apartheid many people were forced into homelands and townships, which are still densely populated.
